fields.sample_size: Single case study of the Chamazi community water and sewerage initiative (Dar es Salaam): fieldwork in March 2013 and March 2015 - one focus group of women's savings-group members (2013), in-depth interviews with 17 evicted households resettled in Chamazi, semi-structured interviews with four officials of the utility DAWASA and Temeke Municipal Council, structured interviews with two officials of the NGO Centre for Community Initiatives, plus field observation and project documents; the case is a federation of about 300 tenant households evicted from Kurasini (about 36,000 inhabitants were served eviction notices in 2006)
fields.effect_measure: qualitative case study; no quantitative estimate
fields.effect_estimate: State compensation went only to structure owners although about 70 per cent of the evicted Kurasini households were tenants. The tenants' savings federation (about 300 households, mostly women) saved for three years, bought 30 acres at Chamazi (about 20 km away and beyond the municipal water and sewer networks) under a collective block title, had the land surveyed and certified by Temeke Municipal Council, and built its own services: a borehole drilled for US$3,000 (Homeless International) with a US$4,000 solar pump (WaterAid with the council) and an on-site sewage treatment plant; water was free for house building and then sold for a small fee, raising about US$2,800 by 2015 for maintenance. The author reads this as grassroots agency instigating institutional change and argues that secure land tenure underpins infrastructure investment (outside utilities feared investing where eviction was possible). No household-level access statistics were found in the text.
